### 4.4.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Facing the destructive reality of artificial intelligence-driven undue influence, doctrinal reconstruction in civil law is no longer merely an academic option, but an urgent historical necessity (Hesselink, 2011; Smits, 2017). We can no longer sustain a narrow interpretation of Articles 1321 and 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*), nor uphold the classical 19th-century principle of freedom of contract that naively ignores digital cognitive asymmetries (Kennedy, 1998; Atiyah, 1979). New doctrinal constructions must broaden the scope of *misbruik van omstandigheden* and undue influence by incorporating a novel juridical category: **"Algorithmic Vulnerability Exploitation"** (Calo, 2014; Hildebrandt, 2015). Within this doctrinal framework, any contract, gift, testamentary disposition, or civil transaction born from intensive interaction with an AI system—empirically proven to erode the legal subject's mental autonomy—must be classified as a fundamental defect of will, rendering it voidable (*vernietigbaar*) upon the request of the victim or their lawful heirs (Asser, 2006; Van Dunné, 2018).

This doctrinal update must also be fully supported by modern, cross-sectoral legal instruments, such as the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) as well as comprehensive international regulations like the EU AI Act (Regulation EU 2024/1689). The latter explicitly prohibits artificial intelligence systems that deploy subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques to materially distort a person's behavior in a manner that causes, or is likely to cause, physical or psychological harm (EU Parliament, 2024; Government of the Republic of Indonesia, 2022). In the context of substantive civil law, violations of these AI design ethics and technical standards must be translated as tangible indicators of an unlawful act (*onrechtmatige daad* pursuant to Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code; Hesselink, 2011), as well as a solid legal foundation for declaring a flawed legal will null and void. Furthermore, the burden of proof (*onus probandi*) must undergo a progressive shift: if it is objectively established that a testator or donor was in a state of heightened emotional or cognitive vulnerability and interacted intensively with a specific AI system prior to executing the legal act, the beneficiary or platform developer shall bear the burden of proving that no manipulation or cognitive exploitation occurred (Schwenzer et al., 2012; Calo, 2014).
